title: SSL/TLS inspection certificates: who signs, and where the root must be trusted

prose.text: For inspection to work without browser warnings the client has to trust whatever signs the leaf certificate. {{central-authority}} {{per-request-certificates}} So the real question is who is in the chain and where it is installed. {{root-must-be-trusted}}

prose.label: Where the root must be installed.
prose.text: {{own-trust-stores}} {{own-trust-store-remedies}} {{chromeos}} {{root-deployment-channels}} Whether the certificate to install is the root or the intermediate is stated two ways {{divergence:root-or-intermediate-on-workstation}}. The macOS route has a version restriction on the Client Connector side {{divergence:macos-app-profile-scope}}. {{root-download}} {{browser-stores}}

The per-tool commands are in [[zia.ssl-inspection.app-trust-stores]]; three legacy mechanisms are still open {{gap:toolchain-trust-mechanisms}}. The intermediate CA object (protection types, limits, key types, CSR signing, chain upload) is in [[zia.ssl-inspection.intermediate-ca]]. Traffic that never accepts the root at all (pinned apps, IoT, guest networks) is in [[zia.ssl-inspection.uninspectable]]; the settings that govern what a rule does with a bad upstream certificate are in [[zia.ssl-inspection.actions]].

checks.do: Which command installs the root for a given toolchain, taken from a source rather than from memory.

central-authority.statement: The Zscaler Central Authority is a private CA that acts as both root and intermediate for the ZIA service, or as an intermediate under the customer's private CA, and it authorizes Public Service Edges to act as intermediate CAs that issue certificates to end users for their requested destinations.

quotes: In ZIA, the Central Authority is a private CA, acting as both root and intermediate CA for the ZIA service or as an intermediate to your private CA.
The Central Authority authorizes the ZIA Public Service Edges to act as intermediate CAs, issuing certificates to end users for their requested destinations.

per-request-certificates.statement: When inspecting, the Public Service Edge acts as a short-lived intermediate CA and issues a certificate on demand for each requested application, which the browser accepts because the Zscaler trust chain is in the device's certificate store.

quotes: the ZIA Public Service Edge acts as a short-lived intermediate CA. As a user requests a connection, the ZIA Public Service Edge issues certificates on demand for the application.
From the browser’s point of view, the ZIA Public Service Edge certificate is valid for the destination.
because the user or administrator imported the ZIA Public Service Edge trust chain into the device’s certificate store.

root-must-be-trusted.statement: With the default Zscaler intermediate certificate every client must have the Zscaler root certificate installed; otherwise browsers and applications show warnings or the traffic cannot be inspected properly.

quotes: If you use the default Zscaler intermediate certificate, ensure all clients have installed the Zscaler root certificate.
Failure to install the Zscaler root certificate results in warnings from browsers and applications or the inability to inspect the traffic properly.

ca-options.statement: Zscaler offers two CA choices that are functionally equivalent and differ in deployment: Zscaler's own CA, whose root must be installed on machines, or the customer's existing CA with Zscaler as an intermediate, which needs an additional Zscaler subscription but lets clients already holding that root start immediately.

quotes: From a functional standpoint, the two options are equivalent, but there are differences in the deployment of the root CA.
Using your existing CA is an additional subscription with Zscaler.

Your client machines are already preloaded with your root CA certificate, and they can begin to use the ZIA service immediately without additional certificate installations in the client certificate store.
You must decide between using the Zscaler Central Authority (CA) or your own existing CA with Zscaler as an intermediate CA.
You must install Zscaler’s root CA in your machines’ certificate stores to deploy the Zscaler Root CA certificate.

hsm.statement: A customer who will not upload an intermediate certificate to Zscaler nodes can keep the private key in a cloud hardware security module (HSM).

quotes: I’m not willing to upload my own intermediate certificate to Zscaler nodes: Zscaler supports private keys in cloud hardware security modules (HSM).

in-memory.statement: Web transaction content inspection takes place in memory and is never written to disk.

quotes: Web transaction content inspection takes place in memory and is never written to disk.

override-intermediate.statement: An Inspect rule can override the default intermediate CA by choosing another intermediate CA from the list; on Block and Do Not Inspect + Evaluate rules the override appears only when the notification setting is on. In the API this is `overrideDefaultCertificate` with an `sslInterceptionCert` reference.

evidence.after: If you choose the Inspect action, configure the following settings:
quotes: Override Default Intermediate CA Certificate: Select Yes to override the default intermediate Certificate Authority (CA) certificate.
Intermediate CA Certificate: Choose an intermediate CA certificate from the list.

evidence.after: If you choose to evaluate other policies for the traffic, you can configure the following settings:
quotes: Override Default Intermediate CA Certificate: Select Yes to override the default intermediate CA certificate. This field is only available if you have enabled Show Notifications for Blocked Traffic.

evidence.after: If you choose the Block action, you can choose to enable or disable end user notifications:
quotes: Override Default Intermediate CA Certificate: Select Yes to override the default intermediate CA certificate. This field is only available if you have enabled Show End User Notifications.
json:"overrideDefaultCertificate,omitempty"
json:"sslInterceptionCert,omitempty"

own-trust-stores.statement: Some applications keep their own certificate trust store, so installing the Zscaler root in the operating system is not enough: Firefox, Python and developer tooling are the named examples, and for non-browser applications that show SSL errors the check is whether the Zscaler root is installed in the proper repository for them.

quotes: Every OS has a default system root CA certificate store. Some applications host their own certificate trust store and might also need to be updated. Firefox, Python, and Dev environments are common examples.
For SSL inspection to work, the certificate chain must be pre-deployed, which means some of these environments need direct intervention to be compatible.
If using Firefox, make sure to update its root certificate store.
Non-browser applications are getting SSL errors: Check if the Zscaler Root certificate is installed in the proper repository for these applications.

own-trust-store-remedies.statement: For applications with custom trust stores Zscaler recommends installing the Zscaler root (or custom intermediate) certificate into the application's store, manually or with a tool such as SCCM; disabling certificate validation is advised only for short-term testing, and the other alternatives are exempting the developer users' traffic, which the guide calls less desirable, or exempting the destination domains.

quotes: Zscaler recommends handling the applications with custom trust stores by installing the Zscaler root cert (or custom intermediate cert) into the application
This is done manually or automatically via a tool like Microsoft System Center Configuration Manager (SCCM).
You can also disable cert validation, which Zscaler recommends only for short terms and testing.
Alternatively, you can exempt the traffic from developer users (which is less desirable) from SSL inspection.
You can also exempt the destination domains to which these apps connect.

chromeos.statement: ChromeOS does not trust managed or user-installed certificates for OS-level communication, so only user traffic can be inspected; the traffic between the device and Google's ChromeOS services must be exempted, using a custom URL category of the required domains.

quotes: you can only inspect user traffic, and you must exempt the traffic between the device and Google’s ChromeOS services.
Put the list of required exemptions by domain into a custom URL category and then bypass the custom URL category from inspection.
ChromeOS doesn’t trust any managed or user-installed certificates for OS-level communications.

mobile-mdm.statement: Installing the certificate on mobile devices requires Mobile Device Management, which is also commonly the best way to deploy Client Connector.

quotes: Installing the certificate on mobile devices requires Mobile Device Management (MDM) and is also commonly the best way to deploy the Zscaler Client Connector application.

servers-deferred.statement: Server networks are typically left out of the first inspection projects and added once user inspection is mostly done, because the root CA must reach the hosts, their containers and custom-trust-store applications. Zscaler recommends restricting server access to explicitly permitted destinations and blocking all other access.

quotes: Due to the potential complexity, server networks are typically excluded from the initial SSL inspection projects and are deployed when production user inspection is mostly completed.
Regarding servers, the primary challenge is getting the root CA certificate installed on the host machines, as well as any containers and applications which make use of Custom Trust Stores.

Zscaler recommends restricting server access to explicitly permitted destinations and blocking all other access, as this can greatly assist in reducing risk of non-inspection until or after inspection is enabled.

proxy-model.statement: With SSL/TLS Inspection enabled, the Zscaler service functions as a full SSL/TLS (man-in-the-middle) proxy and establishes a separate SSL/TLS tunnel with the user's browser and with the destination server. It sends the browser the Zscaler intermediate certificate or the organization's custom intermediate root, as well as a server certificate signed by the Zscaler intermediate CA, and the browser validates the certificate chain in its certificate store.

quotes: It functions as a full SSL/TLS proxy, or SSL/TLS man-in-the-middle (MITM) proxy.
When you enable SSL/TLS Inspection, the Zscaler service establishes a separate SSL/TLS tunnel with the user’s browser and with the destination server.

It sends the browser the Zscaler intermediate certificate or your organization’s custom intermediate root, as well as a server certificate signed by the Zscaler intermediate Certificate Authority (CA).
The browser validates the certificate chain in the browser's certificate store.

generated-certificate-fields.statement: The Zscaler service dynamically generates and signs the server certificate it presents to the client. The certificate contains the same fields as the original destination server certificate except the issuer distinguished name (DN), which is set to the name of the Zscaler intermediate certificate, and the browser receives it signed by the Zscaler intermediate certificate along with that intermediate certificate.

quotes: The Zscaler service dynamically generates and signs the server certificate that it presents to the client.
This certificate contains the same fields as the original destination server certificate, except for the identifying information of the issuer, called the issuer distinguished name (DN).
The issuer DN is set to the name of the Zscaler intermediate certificate.
The browser receives this certificate signed by the Zscaler intermediate certificate along with the Zscaler intermediate certificate.

generated-certificate-caching.statement: The choosing-CA page says the generated certificate's issuer is set to the organization name and the Zscaler service generates the certificate once per site and caches these certificates on the Public Service Edge for Internet & SaaS (ZIA); the cached certificates are usually valid until their expiration date.
generated-certificate-caching.conditions: The page presents this where it describes a custom intermediate certificate; the quoted sentence itself names only the organization as issuer.

quotes: The certificate issuer is set to the organization name, and the Zscaler service generates the certificate once per site and caches these certificates on the Public Service Edge for Internet & SaaS (ZIA).
These cached certificates are usually valid until their expiration date.

crl-distribution-point.statement: Zscaler-issued certificates (leaf or short-lived issuing CA) contain a CRL Distribution Point (CRLDP) hosted by Zscaler for certificate revocation. The service provides a CRL distribution point for every certificate it generates so client applications can locate the CRLs, and the Zscaler-hosted CRLs provide the serial numbers of revoked certificate issuers.

quotes: Zscaler issued certificates (leaf or short-lived issuing CA) contain a CRL Distribution Point (CRLDP) hosted by Zscaler that provides a mechanism for certification revocation.
The Zscaler service provides a Certificate Revocation List (CRL) distribution point (CDP) for every certificate it generates, so that client applications can locate the CRLs as necessary.
The CRLs are hosted by the Zscaler service and provide the serial numbers of revoked certificate issuers.

root-deployment-channels.statement: The Zscaler service does not install a Zscaler root certificate or a custom root certificate on the user's machine for SSL/TLS Inspection. Customers who use Client Connector for traffic forwarding can use the Client Connector App Profile configuration for Windows and macOS to deploy the certificates; customers without Client Connector on their Windows or macOS machines can push the certificate using Microsoft Active Directory, Group Policy Object or another MDM solution; and the certificates need to be installed manually on Android and iOS devices or with MDM solutions.

quotes: The Zscaler service does not install a Zscaler root certificate or a custom root certificate on the user's machine for SSL/TLS Inspection.

Customers who use Zscaler Client Connector for traffic forwarding can use the Zscaler Client Connector App Profile configuration for Windows and macOS to deploy these certificates on the user's machine.

Customers who do not have Zscaler Client Connector installed on their Windows or macOS machines can push the certificate using Microsoft Active Directory (AD), Microsoft's Group Policy Object (GPO), or another Mobile Device Management (MDM) solution.
The certificates need to be installed manually on Android and iOS devices or using MDM solutions.

root-download.statement: The Zscaler root certificate is downloaded from the Root Certificate field of the View Zscaler Intermediate CA Certificate page, reached from Internet Access > Resources > SSL Intermediate Certificate, as a ZIP file named ZscalerRootCerts.zip.

quotes: From the navigation menu, go to Internet Access > Resources > SSL Intermediate Certificate.
On the View Zscaler Intermediate CA Certificate page, under the Root Certificate field, click Download. The root certificate is downloaded as a ZIP file.
Go to the ZscalerRootCerts.zip file and unzip it.

browser-stores.statement: Firefox browsers do not accept SSL/TLS certificates installed in Internet Explorer browsers, so certificates must be installed on Firefox separately if the organization allows Firefox; Google Chrome uses the same certificate store as Microsoft Edge.

quotes: Firefox browsers do not accept SSL/TLS certificates installed in Internet Explorer browsers.
You must install SSL/TLS certificates on Firefox browsers separately if your organization allows Firefox browsers.
Google Chrome, however, uses the same certificate store as Microsoft Edge.

key-storage-by-type.statement: The service generates a CSR with a key pair and encrypts the private key using AES. The private key is stored securely in the Zscaler Central Authority for the software intermediate certificate and the Zscaler intermediate certificate, and in the cloud HSM solution for the cloud HSM intermediate certificate, while the CSR contains the public key.

quotes: The service generates the CSR with a key pair (i.e., public and private key) and encrypts the private key using AES.

The private key is stored securely in the Zscaler Central Authority (CA) for the software intermediate certificate and Zscaler intermediate certificate and the cloud HSM solution for the cloud HSM intermediate certificate, while the CSR contains the public key.

key-generation.statement: When the administrator of an organization requests a CSR for an intermediate Central Authority, the Zscaler CA generates a 2048-bit private and public key pair. The private key is immediately encrypted with AES encryption using a password, which is not transmitted or stored on disk on any system and is held in the system's memory only.

quotes: When the administrator of an organization requests a CSR for an intermediate Central Authority (CA), the Zscaler CA generates a 2048-bit private and public key pair.
The private key is immediately encrypted with AES encryption using a password.
This ensures that the private key password isn't transmitted or stored on disk on any system; it's stored in the system’s memory only.

key-storage-replication.statement: The Zscaler CA encrypts the private key and stores it in an SQL database that contains the organization's policies, accessible only to the organization by logging in with authorized admin credentials. Any write operation to the CA database is immediately replicated to two other identical CA servers in physically separate locations in the US, and the keys are never in the decrypted state on the CA server after they are encrypted.

quotes: The CA encrypts the private key and stores it in an SQL database that contains your organization’s policies.
The SQL database is accessible only to your organization by logging in with authorized admin credentials.
Any write operation to the CA database is immediately replicated to two other identical CA servers in physically separate locations in the US for rapid disaster recovery.
The keys are never in the decrypted state on the CA server after they are encrypted.

key-distribution.statement: For a user's HTTPS request the Public Service Edge requests the organization's key pair from the CA, which sends the key pair with the organization's intermediate certificate over a 2048-bit TLS connection, only to the requesting Public Service Edge. If a location's traffic is sent to an organization's private Public Service Edge only, the CA sends the private key to the private Public Service Edges only and does not send the keys and intermediate certificate to public Public Service Edges in the Zscaler cloud.

quotes: When a user from your organization tries to access a site that uses HTTPS/SSL/TLS, the Public Service Edge requests your organization’s key pair from the CA.
The CA sends the key pair over a 2048-bit TLS connection to the Public Service Edge, along with your organization’s intermediate certificate.
The CA sends the key pair and certificate only to the requesting Public Service Edge.
If a location’s traffic is sent to an organization’s private Public Service Edge only, then the CA sends the private key to the private Public Service Edges only.
It does not send the organization’s keys and intermediate certificate to public Public Service Edges in the Zscaler cloud.

key-in-service-edge-ram.statement: The Public Service Edge maintains the private key unencrypted in its RAM to generate certificates for the websites the user visits; the safeguarding page says these certificates are dynamically generated each time in RAM and not stored in any storage medium. The Service Edge caches the intermediate certificate it received from the CA until it receives a new one.

quotes: The Public Service Edge maintains the private key unencrypted in its RAM to generate certificates for the websites that the user visits.
These certificates are dynamically generated each time in RAM and not stored in any storage medium.
Additionally, the Public Service Edge caches the intermediate certificate that it received from the CA, until it receives a new intermediate certificate from the CA.

ca-outage-behavior.statement: If all CA servers in a cluster are unavailable due to a catastrophic event while the Public Service Edges are still active, the Public Service Edges continue to perform SSL/TLS Inspection as long as the organization's policies, certificates and keys already reside in their memory; a Public Service Edge without the policy and keys does not decrypt the SSL/TLS traffic. If both the CA and the Public Service Edge are unavailable, the service supports a proxy bypass capability where all traffic is allowed without protection.

quotes: If all CA servers in a cluster are not available due to a catastrophic event and the Public Service Edges are still active, the Public Service Edges continue to perform SSL/TLS Inspection as long as an organization’s policies, certificates and keys already reside in the Public Service Edge’s memory.
If a Public Service Edge does not have the policy and keys for an organization, then the Public Service Edge won't decrypt the SSL/TLS traffic.
In the unlikely event that both the CA and Public Service Edge are not available, the Zscaler service supports a proxy bypass capability where all traffic is allowed without protection.

key-memory-zeroing.statement: A Public Service Edge allocates memory from a special region for all SSL/TLS operations, zeroed as soon as the memory is released (packet buffers and key storage areas); it does not allow a data dump from this area from the command line, and all data is zeroed if a process core must be dumped due to a software error. The page says that due to these precautions the Zscaler cloud is invulnerable to SSL/TLS Heartbleed attacks, and that keys are only ephemerally present in Public Service Edge RAM and zeroed after being unused for a short period of time.

quotes: A Public Service Edge allocates memory from a special region for all SSL/TLS operations.
This region of memory is always zeroed out as soon as the memory is released.
This applies to packet buffers as well as key storage areas.
A Public Service Edge also does not allow a data dump from this area from the command line.
All data is zeroed out if a process core must be dumped due to a software error.
Due to these precautions, the Zscaler cloud is invulnerable to SSL/TLS Heartbleed attacks.

The CA sends SSL/TLS keys only to the Public Service Edges that process your organization’s traffic. They are only ephemerally present in the Public Service Edge RAM and are zeroed out of RAM after they are unused for a short period of time.

key-rotation-and-revocation.statement: When a new intermediate certificate is generated a new key is generated as well, and the old key and intermediate certificate are removed from the database and its backup. The organization sets the certificate's expiration date and can revoke it at any time; administrators cannot use the intermediate certificate issued to Zscaler to sign any other certificate because the private key never leaves the Zscaler CA or Public Service Edge.

quotes: When a new intermediate certificate is generated, a new key is generated as well.
The old key and intermediate certificate are removed from the database, as well as the database backup.
Your organization sets the expiration date for the certificate and can revoke it at any time.
Administrators cannot use the intermediate certificate issued to Zscaler to sign any other certificate because the private key never leaves the Zscaler CA or Public Service Edge.

operations-certifications.statement: Zscaler operation processes and its Information Security Management System (ISMS) are ISO 27001 and SOC 2 Type II certified, all Public Service Edges and CAs are monitored for 24 hours, and access to the CA and Public Service Edges is highly restricted and controlled.

quotes: Zscaler operation processes and its Information Security Management System (ISMS) are ISO 27001 and SOC 2 Type II certified.
All Public Service Edges and CAs are monitored for 24 hours.
Access to the CA and Public Service Edges is highly restricted and controlled.

ca-choice-not-a-match-criterion.statement: Neither CA choice changes how SSL inspection rules match: the rule match expression has no CA or certificate term.
ca-choice-not-a-match-criterion.conditions: Assumes operator-expression lists every matching dimension; an Inspect rule's intermediate CA override is an action setting, not a match term.

generated-certificate-lifetime.summary: The safeguarding page says the certificates are dynamically generated each time in RAM and not stored; the choosing-CA page says the service generates the certificate once per site and caches it on the Public Service Edge.

quotes: These certificates are dynamically generated each time in RAM and not stored in any storage medium.

positions.says: Certificates are generated each time in RAM and not stored in any storage medium.

quotes: The certificate issuer is set to the organization name, and the Zscaler service generates the certificate once per site and caches these certificates on the Public Service Edge for Internet & SaaS (ZIA).

positions.says: With the certificate issuer set to the organization name (the custom-intermediate case), the service generates the certificate once per site and caches it on the Public Service Edge.

generated-certificate-lifetime.impact: Whether each connection gets a new certificate or a cached one differs between the pages, and the second is written for the organization-issuer case. The existing claim per-request-certificates (certificates issued on demand for the application) is compatible with either, and the gap leaf-per-connection stays open.

intermediate-key-size.summary: The safeguarding page says the Zscaler CA generates a 2048-bit key pair for an intermediate CA CSR; the Software Protection and Cloud HSM Protection pages say the key size can be RSA 2048 or EC P-256.

quotes: the Zscaler CA generates a 2048-bit private and public key pair.

positions.says: The Zscaler CA generates a 2048-bit private and public key pair.

quotes: Key Type: Select the key size from the drop-down menu. The key size can be RSA 2048 or EC P-256.
The EC P-256 option is available if Custom Certificate Compliance is enabled for your organization.

positions.says: The key size can be RSA 2048 or EC P-256, and EC P-256 is available if Custom Certificate Compliance is enabled (the Cloud HSM Protection page says the same; see zia.ssl-inspection.intermediate-ca:key-type-and-signature).

intermediate-key-size.impact: An organization with Custom Certificate Compliance enabled can choose EC P-256, which a 2048-bit statement does not cover; the safeguarding page does not mention the option.

root-or-intermediate-on-workstation.summary: The choosing-CA page says users must install the Zscaler intermediate CA certificate on their workstations and, on the same page, that the organization does not need to install it because the service sends it with the generated certificate; its download steps give the root certificate.

quotes: your users must install the Zscaler intermediate CA certificate on their workstations.

positions.says: Users must install the Zscaler intermediate CA certificate on their workstations.

quotes: Your organization does not need to install the Zscaler intermediate certificate because the Zscaler service sends it together with the certificate the service generated for the destination site.
The root certificate is downloaded as a ZIP file.

positions.says: The intermediate certificate need not be installed because the service sends it with the generated certificate; the download steps give the root certificate.

quotes: If you use the default Zscaler intermediate certificate, ensure all clients have installed the Zscaler root certificate.

positions.says: With the default Zscaler intermediate certificate, clients must have the Zscaler root certificate installed (existing claim root-must-be-trusted).

root-or-intermediate-on-workstation.impact: Which certificate an administrator has to put on workstations is stated two ways on one page; the root reading agrees with root-must-be-trusted.

macos-app-profile-scope.summary: The choosing-CA page says the Client Connector App Profile can deploy the certificates for Windows and macOS; the Client Connector page says Install Zscaler SSL Certificate is not supported on macOS Big Sur (11) and later.

quotes: Customers who use Zscaler Client Connector for traffic forwarding can use the Zscaler Client Connector App Profile configuration for Windows and macOS to deploy these certificates on the user's machine.

positions.says: The Client Connector App Profile configuration for Windows and macOS can deploy the certificates.

quotes: Install Zscaler SSL Certificate is not supported on devices running macOS Big Sur (11) and later.

positions.says: Install Zscaler SSL Certificate is not supported on macOS Big Sur (11) and later (zcc.ssl-inspection.certificate-install:big-sur).

macos-app-profile-scope.impact: The macOS route in root-deployment-channels does not carry the Big Sur and later restriction that zcc.ssl-inspection.certificate-install states for the Install Zscaler SSL Certificate setting; the pages do not say whether the App Profile route is affected.

leaf-per-connection.title: Whether each inspected connection gets its own ephemeral leaf certificate valid for the destination hostname/SAN
leaf-per-connection.detail: Unverified legacy statement: 'The client receives a fresh leaf cert per session, signed by Zscaler's CA, valid for the destination's hostname/SAN. There is no long-lived Zscaler-as-the-server cert; each connection gets its own ephemeral leaf.' The help pages now say the generated certificate has the same fields as the original destination server certificate except the issuer DN, and disagree on whether it is generated each time or once per site and cached (divergence generated-certificate-lifetime); lifetime and SAN contents beyond 'same fields' are not stated.

deployment-channels.title: Named deployment channel for the root certificate that no page names (Android EMM)
deployment-channels.detail: Unverified legacy statement: 'MDM (Intune, Jamf, Android EMM) for mobile + ZCC bundling'. The choosing-CA page now names Active Directory, Group Policy Object, Client Connector App Profile and 'another MDM' (root-deployment-channels), which settles the GPO path; ZIA_SSL_Inspection_Leading_Practices_Guide.txt names MDM and SCCM only. Jamf Pro and Intune are covered by zcc.ssl-inspection.certificate-install:macos-mdm-profile; no captured page names Android EMM.

toolchain-trust-mechanisms.title: Toolchain trust-store mechanisms the trust-store article does not give (PIP_CERT, the .npmrc file, Docker certs.d)
toolchain-trust-mechanisms.detail: Most per-toolchain mechanisms (Firefox security.enterprise_roots.enabled, REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE, certifi, NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS, npm cafile, Git http.sslcainfo, Java keytool into cacerts) are now claims in zia.ssl-inspection.app-trust-stores. Still unverified from the legacy statement: `PIP_CERT` (the article uses `pip config set global.cert`), the `.npmrc` file name (the article uses `npm config set cafile`), and Docker certs under `/etc/docker/certs.d/` plus restart (the article installs into the container's OpenSSL store).
toolchain-trust-mechanisms.blocks: telling a developer exactly how to trust the Zscaler root in a given toolchain
